DESI · Instrumentation analysis

Differential Atmospheric Refraction and Fiber Flux Loss at High Airmass

Two findings from the standard-star calibration data: a flux-loss calibration shift that turned on around mid-2025 (not the PlateMaker), and a residual-DAR limit at high airmass with real observing-strategy consequences.

K. Honscheid OSUwith Claude Anthropic2026‑07‑23

Detection, mechanism, and observing-strategy implications — from the pooled calibstars dataset plus a per-exposure pointing/timing table joined from the KPNO exposure DB. Reproduces from notebooks/dar_fiber_loss_reproduction.ipynb and notebooks/dar_pointing_tests.ipynb.

Two findings

  1. A flux-loss calibration shift turned on around mid-2025 — and nobody had flagged it. Standard-star loss stepped up across all airmass, including low airmass where DAR is negligible (0.12→0.70 ×10⁻³), so it is a change in the flux-loss calibration itself. A three-epoch split shows it is not the March-2026 PlateMaker change (loss unchanged across it at every airmass). Flagged to Data Systems; origin not diagnosed here.
  2. The steep growth of loss with airmass is residual DAR acting during the exposure. DESI's fixed, airmass-driven ADC removes the bulk; what remains forms a focal-plane dipole that rotates with the parallactic angle — driven near the meridian by the rotation of the refraction offset, off it by the magnitude change the fixed ADC can't track. It scales as tan z · dq/dt · T, is largely irreducible by positioning, and is invisible to short dither sequences. Proximity to transit is the dominant lever, and the ADC's ZD = 60° limit makes Dec ≤ −28° a qualitatively harder regime.

Part I · The detection

1 When did the loss change?

The alarm came from a two-epoch before/after split at the PlateMaker date. Before reading anything physical into it, we asked simply when the loss changed. Mean loss vs time, split by airmass:

Three things read off it: the rise is airmass-graded (high > mid > low); even low airmass lifts off its flat pre-2025 baseline, so a genuine systematic sits underneath where DAR is negligible; and there is no step at the PlateMaker line — the climb is underway well before 2026-03-07. To sharpen it, split into three epochs — A before 2025-03 (flat baseline), B to the 2026-03-07 change, C after:

airmassA (<2025-03)B (2025-03→2026-03)C (>2026-03)
1.0–1.2  low, DAR-free0.12 [0.08, 0.15]0.70 [0.64, 0.76]0.67 [0.57, 0.76]
1.5–2.05  high0.97 [0.74, 1.16]4.11 [3.83, 4.39]3.89 [3.12, 4.59]

mean loss ×10⁻³, bootstrap-over-exposures 16–84% intervals.

2 It is calibration-level — not the PlateMaker, not purely DAR

  • A→B is a large, significant jump at both airmasses (low ~6×, high ~4×; intervals nowhere near overlapping) — the mid-2025 systematic.
  • B→C is null (0.70 vs 0.67; 4.11 vs 3.89; intervals overlap): the PlateMaker change added nothing at any airmass.
  • The low-airmass jump is the key. Where DAR is negligible, positioning and atmosphere cannot create a loss, yet the loss still rose A→B — isolating a calibration- / measurement-level change around mid-2025.

Something in the flux-loss calibration changed around mid-2025. We flag it to Data Systems and do not diagnose its origin: it need not be an offline-pipeline change — a genuine instrument or software effect would look the same. What the split establishes firmly: the increase is not the PlateMaker (B ≈ C) and not purely DAR (it appears at low airmass). The original before/after “excess” was an artifact of a two-epoch split straddling this transition. The rest of the report addresses the independent question — why loss grows with airmass in every epoch — which is residual DAR.

Part II · The mechanism

3 DESI's ADC removes the bulk — we measure the residual

DESI actively corrects DAR: the exposure record carries a two-element atmospheric dispersion corrector (ADC), and the data show it is real, active, and airmass-driven (n = 12,043):

  • Prism separation angle correlates with airmass at ρ = 0.996 — rising from ~12.5° near zenith to ~116° at high airmass. Textbook counter-rotating dual-prism behavior: separation sets the amount of dispersion correction.
  • The prisms are STOPPED (fixed) for the whole exposure — both statuses STOPPED for 100% of exposures, and no adc_rate field exists (unlike the continuously-driven rotator). Set once, held.

Two consequences frame everything below. (i) A fixed ADC cannot adapt to airmass continuing to change during the exposure — a specific mechanism for the intra-exposure, time-accumulating residual. (ii) The bulk, achromatic, zenith-aligned DAR is already removed, so the residual is smaller and need not reproduce the naive “uncorrected DAR” shape. (The assumption “ADC set near exposure start” is a strong circumstantial case, not independently validated for when it is set.)

4 The residual loss pattern is DAR

Binned by airmass, the focal-plane loss shows a coherent N–S dipole strengthening steeply with airmass (before top, after bottom).

(a) It matches the equatorial-mount prediction — a dipole (tilt) with amplitude ∝ tan z·sec² z along the N–S axis, both confirmed by fitting the tilt per airmass bin.

(b) The dipole rotates with the parallactic angle — the decisive test, enabled by the new pointing data. If the tilt is DAR its direction must track q; an instrumental tilt would not.

5 Near the meridian it is the rotation, not the airmass change

With perfect instantaneous positioning, the residual loss comes from how the DAR offset changes as the telescope tracks. The parallactic angle q is the position angle of the zenith; the offset (magnitude ∝ tan z) points at PA = q.

The offset changes two ways: magnitude (rate ∝ sec²z·dz/dt, dz/dt∝sin H — zero at the meridian) and direction (rate ∝ tan z·dq/dt, dq/dt=ωcosφ/sin z at transit — near-maximal at the meridian). So near the meridian the magnitude is frozen and the rotation dominates, drift rate

tan z·dq/dt = ω·cosφ·sec z

present at transit and growing as sec z = airmass. Distinctive prediction: the residual loss is present at the meridian and grows with airmass — opposite to an off-meridian magnitude drift. (A small field-rotation channel is actively compensated by the hexapod rotator; the DAR-dispersion drift is the uncorrected driver.)

6 Two spatial views, reconciled: isotropic monopole vs. rotating dipole

An earlier decomposition by distance from field center found something that looked, at first, like the opposite of DAR — worth reconciling explicitly.

The radial (monopole) gradient is large and isotropic, and it flattens with airmass; a validated zenith-direction decomposition shows the signed along-zenith term explains almost nothing (R² = 0.0007 vs 0.132). But the dipole, once isolated, is directional DAR, and it is threshold-like: the along-zenith signal is ~0 below airmass 1.4, rising to clearly positive at airmass ≥ 1.8, near the ADC's limit.

These are different multipoles of the same maps, and they agree. The isotropic radial monopole is a static field pattern plus seeing (§8), the ADC having removed the bulk directional DAR. The dipole is the residual directional DAR, small at typical airmass and growing near the ADC limit. The new pointing data (§4) is exactly this dipole seen with the parallactic angle attached: the radial view inferred “directional DAR turns on at airmass ≥ 1.8,” and Test A confirms it directly — the dipole rotates with q.

7 The residual accumulates over the exposure — two faces

That the effect is intra-exposure (accumulating with time, not a fixed offset) shows up in two complementary observables.

(a) Mean loss — the rotation-drift channel, strongest near transit. Loss peaks at the meridian (dq/dt) and grows ~2.6× for 2× the exposure time at fixed seeing & airmass — genuinely time-integrated.

(b) Within-exposure scatter — the magnitude-change / ADC-mismatch channel, strongest off transit. Star-to-star scatter grows with how much airmass actually changes during the exposure, |Δairmass| (R² 0.096→0.144→0.204 on the complete population): the fixed ADC's one-shot correction increasingly misses as airmass evolves, smearing the flux distribution.

The two faces are one residual, split by hour angle. Near transit the magnitude is frozen but dq/dt is maximal → the rotation channel (mean-loss dipole). Off transit dq/dt falls but |Δairmass| grows → the magnitude-change channel (scatter). Both are residual DAR after a fixed ADC, both accumulate with time, both grow with airmass.

8 Seeing drives the isotropic radial pattern

The zenith decomposition ruled out a coherent DAR shift as the cause of the isotropic radial pattern, leaving the mechanism open. Seeing — a complete per-exposure scalar only weakly correlated with airmass (ρ = 0.098, separable) — is the answer: radius × seeing reproduces the same flattening signature and explains slightly more (R² = 0.140 vs 0.132), and combined, each retains an independent, highly significant contribution. A general (non-directional) PSF-broadening effect — exactly why it does not align with the zenith direction the way DAR would — interacting with some radially-varying fiber-coupling sensitivity not yet localized. Unlike airmass, seeing has a stochastic weather component, so live seeing could inform exposure-time decisions alongside geometry.

Part III · Observing-strategy implications

9 Largely irreducible, and invisible to dither validation

Irreducible by positioning (Dec −25°, 20-min exposure, airmass ~1.85, fiber 300 mm from center):

quantityvalue
target drift over the exposure (parallactic rotation ~5°)~28 μm
residual RMS even with perfect midpoint positioning~8 μm
midpoint − integrated-loss-optimal position~0.1 μm

The midpoint already coincides with the integrated-loss optimum to ~0.1 μm, so re-optimizing the fiber position gains nothing. Invisible to dither validation: positioning is validated with short (3-min) repositioned exposures over which no rotation drift accumulates, so the dithers cannot see this by construction. (The March-2026 second-order refraction term improves that instantaneous metric — a real improvement — but does not bound the intra-exposure drift; track the two separately.)

10 Proximity to transit is the dominant lever

Since the mean-loss channel peaks at the meridian, one might hope to observe a given field off-meridian, trading airmass for lower dq/dt. It does the opposite. For a fixed field the drift is minimized at transit: off-meridian dq/dt falls but tan z rises (product ~flat) and the previously-zero magnitude drift switches on, so the total only increases. A 20-min exposure at Dec −25° drifts ~26 μm at transit, ~35 at HA = 1 h, ~75 at 2 h. Transit is already the optimal hour angle.

The scatter channel agrees: at matched current airmass, an off-transit field accumulates |Δairmass| ~30× faster (Dec −5° 38° off transit: Δ = +0.064 in 10 min; Dec −20° at transit: +0.002). A deep-south field near transit can be safer than a moderate-Dec field well off transit. The answer to “does it depend only on airmass?” is no — proximity to transit matters as much as or more than Dec, and this follows from exact geometry.

Dectransit airmass±2°±4°±6°±8°
−5°1.25+1%+1%+1%+3%
−15°1.47+7%+7%+7%+7%
−20°1.62+12%+12%+7%+13%
−24°1.79+12%+12%too little data
−25° & south1.83+no data at any window width

Scatter increase vs symmetric HA half-window (baseline 0.0422). Within Dec ≥ −22° the excursion channel stays modest; there is a hard data wall at Dec ≈ −24°/−25°.

11 The ADC ZD = 60° wall constrains the southern program

The ADC has a hard limit at ZD = 60° (airmass 2.0): only 3/12,043 exposures exceed it, with a saturated, flat prism angle. At KPNO's latitude the best-case airmass is sec(|lat−Dec|) at transit:

DecZD at transitairmass at transit
−20°51.96°1.62
−25°56.96°1.83
−28°59.96°2.00 — the ADC's limit
−30°61.96°2.13
−35°66.96°2.56

Dec ≈ −28° is the critical threshold. Fields at Dec ≤ −28° never drop below ZD = 60° even at transit — their entire observation runs where the ADC cannot fully correct, so loss there is substantially uncorrected DAR (a qualitatively larger effect), and it is exactly where the directional dipole turns on. Quantifying it needs a targeted Dec ≤ −28° sample, which does not exist yet (the southern program is just beginning). An empirical, non-extrapolated lookup shows the best-populated near-limit cell (airmass 1.8–2.0, large |Δairmass|, n = 45) at ~2× the low-airmass baseline scatter.

12 What to do with this

  • Schedule long/southern exposures to straddle transit as tightly as feasible — the single most effective lever, grounded in exact geometry.
  • Cap exposure duration at high airmass — drift accumulates ∝ T; weigh the ~1–2% loss against the ~2-min-per-restart overhead (cost/benefit needs the science-value of a given scatter increase, out of scope here).
  • Treat Dec ≤ −28° as an under-corrected regime; revisit with a targeted sample as the southern survey accumulates.
  • Track instantaneous-positioning and intra-exposure loss separately — dither validation does not bound the latter.
  • Don't rely on positioning to fix the rotation drift — the midpoint is already the integrated-loss optimum.

Full detail, the investigation history (snapshot-airmass correction, 22% population fix, region/season checks), and a status table for every finding are in DAR_FIBER_LOSS_REPORT.md.
